--- title: "Bayesian Neural Posterior Estimation" description: "Neural posterior estimation, and its Bayesian version with a prior on the network weights: how a network learns the posterior from simulations, and calibrated posteriors from small simulation budgets." categories: [Simulation-based inference, Neural Networks] order: 41 reading-time: true --- ## General Principles ### Simulation-based inference Many models can be written down and simulated, but not integrated: the likelihood $p(x \mid \theta)$ has no closed form, so Bayes' theorem cannot be applied directly. *Simulation-based inference* replaces the likelihood by simulations drawn from the prior predictive distribution, $\theta_j \sim p(\theta)$ and $x_j \sim p(x \mid \theta_j)$, and approximates the posterior from them. Three families are available in BF: Approximate Bayesian Computation keeps the simulations whose summary statistics are close to those of the data ([chapter 38](38.%20Approximate%20Bayesian%20Computation.qmd)); ABC with random forests replaces that acceptance step by a regression on a reference table ([chapter 39](39.%20ABC%20random%20forests.qmd)); Neural Posterior Estimation trains a network on *all* the simulations ([chapter 40](40.%20Neural%20Posterior%20Estimation.qmd)). This chapter is the fourth one, Bayesian Neural Posterior Estimation: NPE with a prior on the network weights. It is written to be read on its own; chapters 38 to 40 are only pointed to for the comparisons. ### Neural Posterior Estimation in brief Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) *learns* the posterior instead of sampling or rejecting it [@papamakarios2016fast]: 1) Simulate many pairs $(\theta, x)$ from the model: $\theta$ from the prior, then a dataset $x$ given $\theta$. 2) Train a neural network $q_\phi(\theta \mid x)$, a conditional density estimator, to predict the distribution of $\theta$ from the (summary statistics of the) data $x$. 3) Evaluate the trained network at the observed data: $q_\phi(\theta \mid x_{obs})$ approximates the posterior $p(\theta \mid x_{obs})$. Because every simulation is used (none is rejected), NPE typically needs far fewer simulations than ABC. And because the network has learned the posterior for *every* possible dataset, it is **amortized**: once trained, the posterior of a new dataset costs one forward pass, with no new simulations. ### The problem: over-confident posteriors The weakness of NPE appears when simulations are expensive and the budget is small: the network over-fits the few training pairs and returns posteriors that are *too narrow*, i.e., credible intervals that contain the true parameter less often than they claim [@hermans2022trust]. The network is then too sure of itself, which is the dangerous side of the error. ### Bayesian Neural Posterior Estimation Bayesian NPE (BNPE) applies the idea of Bayesian neural networks to NPE [@delaunoy2024low]: instead of committing to one trained network, it treats the weights of the network as unknown quantities, exactly as a Bayesian model treats a parameter. The recipe is: 1) Train a standard NPE network on the simulations. 2) Treat its weights $\phi$ as random variables with a prior, and approximate their posterior given the simulations, $p(\phi \mid \mathcal{D})$, with variational inference. 3) Average the posterior estimates of many networks drawn from $p(\phi \mid \mathcal{D})$. With few simulations, many networks are compatible with the data, so the average is wide: BNPE trades sharpness for *calibration*, and its credible intervals are conservative rather than over-confident. As the budget grows, $p(\phi \mid \mathcal{D})$ concentrates and BNPE converges to NPE. ## How NPE is trained `m.npe()` performs the following steps; the *From scratch* tab of the example below writes them out with BF functions. 1. **Simulation.** $M$ pairs (`num_simulations`) are drawn from the prior predictive distribution: $\theta_j \sim p(\theta)$, $x_j \sim p(x \mid \theta_j)$, $s_j = s(x_j)$. Pairs with non-finite values are dropped. 2. **Unconstrained parameters.** Each parameter is mapped to the real line by the bijection of its prior support, $u_j = T^{-1}(\theta_j)$ (here $u = (\alpha,\ \log\beta,\ \text{logit}(\sigma/50))$). The network models $q(u \mid s)$, so every sample $\theta = T(u)$ automatically respects the support. 3. **Standardisation.** Targets and inputs are standardised with the means and standard deviations of the training set: $\tilde u = (u - \bar u)/\text{sd}(u)$ and $\tilde s = (s - \bar s)/\text{sd}(s)$. The density of the original $u$ includes the Jacobian of this rescaling: $\log q(u \mid s) = \log \tilde q(\tilde u \mid \tilde s) - \sum_d \log \text{sd}(u_d)$. 4. **Training.** 10% of the pairs are held out for validation. The network is trained with Adam (learning rate `lr`) on mini-batches of `batch_size` pairs; every 200 steps the validation loss is computed, the best network so far is kept, and training stops when the validation loss has not improved for `patience` evaluations, or after `max_steps` steps. 5. **Posterior.** For the observed data, $\tilde s_{obs}$ is fed to the network, `num_samples` draws $\tilde u \sim \tilde q(\cdot \mid \tilde s_{obs})$ are un-standardised and mapped back with $\theta = T(u)$. `m.npe_posterior(x_new)` repeats this step for a new dataset, without new simulations. Two density estimators are available through `estimator`: a *mixture density network* (default, `"mdn"`), the posterior is a mixture of `n_components` multivariate Normal distributions whose weights, means and covariances are outputs of a neural network built with BF's BNN layers; or a conditional *normalizing flow* (`"flow"`), a chain of `n_layers` invertible transformations of a Normal distribution, more flexible for strongly non-Gaussian posteriors. Both are written explicitly in the *Mathematical Details* below. ### The same network as a BF model The from-scratch code trains the same network as a BF model. With Normal priors on the weights, $W^{(l)} \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1/\sqrt{n_{in}^{(l)}})$ and $b^{(l)} \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1)$, SVI with a point-mass guide (`AutoDelta`) finds the posterior mode of the weights, $$ \hat\phi = \arg\max_\phi \left[\sum_{j=1}^{M} \log q_\phi(u_j \mid s_j) + \log p(\phi)\right], $$ i.e. the NPE loss plus a weight decay ($\log p(\phi)$ is a sum of squared weights). Each SVI step uses a random mini-batch $B$ of 256 simulations (`m.dist.plate(..., subsample_size=256)`), whose log-likelihood is rescaled by $M/|B|$, for a fixed number of steps instead of early stopping. Posterior draws of a new dataset are predictions of the trained model: `m.sample()` runs the network on $\tilde s$ and draws $u$ from the mixture. This is the bridge to Bayesian NPE: the same model stays, and only the variational family of `m.svi` changes, from a point mass to a distribution over the weights. ## Considerations ::: callout-note **Neural posterior estimation** - The model is written as in any BF chapter; `m.npe()` uses it only as a simulator. As in ABC, the data are summarized with `summary_stats` (a function, or `"identity"`, `"moments"`, `"quantiles"`, `"robust"`). NPE copes with more statistics than ABC, since the network learns which ones matter. - `estimator` chooses the density estimator: `"mdn"` (default, mixture density network) or `"flow"` (normalizing flow). - Parameters are learned in the unconstrained space of their prior support and transformed back, so constraints such as $\sigma > 0$ always hold. - A posterior estimated by NPE must be **checked for calibration**. `m.sbc_coverage()` simulates new $(\theta^*, x^*)$ pairs and measures how often $\theta^*$ falls in the $\alpha\%$ highest-posterior-density region: a calibrated posterior lies on the diagonal, an over-confident one below it [@hermans2022trust]. - With small simulation budgets, NPE posteriors tend to be over-confident: Bayesian NPE, below, addresses this. **Bayesian NPE** - Bayesian NPE is NPE with `bayesian=True`: `m.npe(model, ..., bayesian=True)`. Everything else (summary statistics, transforms, density estimator) is as above. - **Weight prior**: weights of a layer with $n_{in}$ inputs are $\text{Normal}(0, \sigma_\phi/\sqrt{n_{in}})$ and biases $\text{Normal}(0, \sigma_\phi)$, with $\sigma_\phi$ = `prior_scale` (default 1). - **Inference on the weights**: a mean-field Normal variational distribution, fitted with stochastic variational inference (`svi_steps` Adam steps) and initialised at the weights of the trained standard network. Full MCMC on thousands of network weights is far too slow and does not mix between the many equivalent modes of a neural network posterior. - **Posterior estimate**: the average of the mixture densities of `num_weight_samples` networks drawn from the weight posterior. - Always compare calibration with `m.sbc_coverage()`: NPE below the diagonal (over-confident) and BNPE on or above it (calibrated or conservative) is the expected picture with small budgets. ::: ## Example Below is an example code snippet demonstrating *Bayesian Neural Posterior Estimation* using the BayesForge (**BF**) package, on the linear regression of height on weight of [chapter 1](1.%20Linear%20Regression%20for%20continuous%20variable.qmd) [@mcelreath2018statistical], with the least-squares intercept, slope and residual standard deviation as summary statistics. The simulation budget is deliberately small: 1 000 simulated datasets. NPE and BNPE are trained on them, and their calibration is checked on 200 new simulated datasets. The *From scratch* tab builds the Bayesian network directly with BF's BNN layers (`m.bnn.layer_linear` and the output layer `m.bnn.layer_mixture_normal`), BF distributions as weight priors, and BF's stochastic variational inference (`m.svi`); the *Built-in function* tab obtains the same result with `m.npe(bayesian=True)` and `m.sbc_coverage()`. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Python ::: {#68c2a999 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from BayesForge import bf import jax import jax.numpy as jnp import numpyro import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # Setup device------------------------------------------------ m = bf(platform="cpu", rand_seed=0) # Import Data & Data Manipulation ------------------------------------------------ data_path = m.load.howell1(only_path=True) m.data(data_path, sep=";") m.df = m.df[m.df.age > 18] # Subset data to adults m.scale(["weight"]) # Normalize # Define model ------------------------------------------------ def model(weight, height): a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, name="a") b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 1, name="b") s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, name="s") m.dist.normal(a + b * weight, s, obs=height) # Summary statistics ------------------------------------------------ weight = jnp.asarray(m.df.weight.values) height_obs = jnp.asarray(m.df.height.values) X = jnp.stack([jnp.ones_like(weight), weight], axis=1) def ols(height): """Least-squares intercept, slope and residual sd: sufficient for this model.""" coef = jnp.linalg.lstsq(X, height)[0] return jnp.array([coef[0], coef[1], jnp.std(height - X @ coef)]) # Reference: exact posterior with MCMC ------------------------------------------------ m.fit(model, progress_bar=False) nuts = dict(m.posteriors) howell = {"weight": weight, "height": height_obs} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` jax.local_device_count 16 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} #### From scratch Bayesian NPE written out with BF functions only. The network is a BF model: its weights are `m.dist.normal` priors, its layers `m.bnn.layer_linear`, and its output layer `m.bnn.layer_mixture_normal` is the likelihood of the simulated parameters. The *same* model gives both estimators; only the guide of BF's stochastic variational inference (`m.svi`) changes: a point-mass guide (`AutoDelta`) gives standard NPE (one network), and a mean-field Normal guide (`AutoNormal`), started at the NPE network, gives Bayesian NPE (a distribution over networks). Posterior draws are predictions of the model (`m.sample`), one per network draw. ::: {#36066365 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np from numpyro.infer import Trace_ELBO, log_likelihood from numpyro.infer.autoguide import AutoDelta, AutoNormal from numpyro.infer.initialization import init_to_sample, init_to_value # 1. Simulations: 1 000 for training, 200 to test calibration ------------------------- M, M_test = 1_000, 200 a = m.dist.normal(178, 20, sample=True, shape=(M + M_test,)) b = m.dist.log_normal(0, 1, sample=True, shape=(M + M_test,)) s = m.dist.uniform(0, 50, sample=True, shape=(M + M_test,)) height = m.dist.normal(a[:, None] + b[:, None] * weight, s[:, None], sample=True) stats = jax.vmap(ols)(height) # 2. Unconstrained parameters, standardised with the training set --------------------- u = jnp.stack([a, jnp.log(b), jax.scipy.special.logit(s / 50)], axis=1) u_mean, u_sd = u[:M].mean(0), u[:M].std(0) s_mean, s_sd = stats[:M].mean(0), stats[:M].std(0) un, sn = (u - u_mean) / u_sd, (stats - s_mean) / s_sd def to_params(u_std): u = u_std * u_sd + u_mean return {"a": u[:, 0], "b": jnp.exp(u[:, 1]), "s": 50 * jax.nn.sigmoid(u[:, 2])} # 3. The network as a BF model: weight priors, BNN layers, mixture likelihood ------- D, K, H = 3, 5, 64 sizes = [3, H, H, m.bnn.mixture_normal_size(K, D)] def npe_net(c, u=None, batch_size=None): params = [(m.dist.normal(0, 1 / jnp.sqrt(n_in), shape=(n_in, n_out), name=f"W{i}"), m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(n_out,), name=f"b{i}")) for i, (n_in, n_out) in enumerate(zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:]))] with m.dist.plate("sims", c.shape[0], subsample_size=batch_size) as idx: h = c[idx] for i, (W, bias) in enumerate(params): act = "gelu" if i < len(params) - 1 else None h = m.bnn.layer_linear(h, W, activation=act, bias=bias, verbose=False) m.bnn.layer_mixture_normal(h, K, D, diag_offset=0.5413, name="u", obs=u if u is None else u[idx]) m.data_on_model = {"c": sn[:M], "u": un[:M], "batch_size": 256} ``` ::: ::: {#28497ce9 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # 4. NPE: point estimate of the weights (AutoDelta) ----------------------------------- m.svi(npe_net, guide=AutoDelta(npe_net, init_loc_fn=init_to_sample), optim=numpyro.optim.Adam(1e-3), loss=Trace_ELBO(), num_steps=10_000, num_samples=100) w_npe = dict(m.posteriors) # 100 copies of one network # 5. Bayesian NPE: Normal distribution over the weights (AutoNormal), from the NPE network start = {name: draws[0] for name, draws in w_npe.items()} m.svi(npe_net, guide=AutoNormal(npe_net, init_loc_fn=init_to_value(values=start), init_scale=1e-3), optim=numpyro.optim.Adam(1e-3), loss=Trace_ELBO(), num_steps=10_000, num_samples=100) w_bnpe = dict(m.posteriors) # 100 different networks ``` ::: ::: {#7f2b6d7a .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # 6. Posterior draws (m.sample) and densities (average over the network draws) -------- def draw(weights, c, n_per_net): """Posterior draws for each row of c: n_per_net per network -> (rows, 100 * n_per_net, D).""" data = {"c": jnp.repeat(c, n_per_net, axis=0), "u": None, "batch_size": None} u = m.sample(posterior_draws=weights, data=data)["u"] # (100 nets, rows * n, D) u = u.reshape(100, c.shape[0], n_per_net, D) return jnp.moveaxis(u, 0, 1).reshape(c.shape[0], -1, D) def log_q(weights, n_nets, u, c): """log of the average density over n_nets network draws, for rows (u, c).""" w = {name: draws[:n_nets] for name, draws in weights.items()} ll = log_likelihood(npe_net, w, c=c, u=u)["u"] # (n_nets, rows) return jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(ll, axis=0) - jnp.log(n_nets) estimators = {"NPE": (w_npe, 1), "BNPE": (w_bnpe, 100)} # 7. Posterior of the observed data ---------------------------------------------------- c_obs = (ols(height_obs) - s_mean) / s_sd raw = {name: to_params(draw(w, c_obs[None], 10)[0]) for name, (w, _) in estimators.items()} for name, post in raw.items(): print(name, {p: f"{post[p].mean():.2f} ± {post[p].std():.2f}" for p in ["a", "b", "s"]}) # 8. Expected coverage on the 200 test simulations ------------------------------------ u_test, c_test = un[M:], sn[M:] levels = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 50) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 4.5)) ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=1) for name, (w, n_nets) in estimators.items(): draws = draw(w, c_test, 5) # (200, 500, D) ranks = [] for i in range(0, M_test, 10): # 10 test sets at a time u_d, c_d = draws[i:i + 10], c_test[i:i + 10] lq_draws = log_q(w, n_nets, u_d.reshape(-1, D), jnp.repeat(c_d, 500, axis=0)).reshape(-1, 500) lq_true = log_q(w, n_nets, u_test[i:i + 10], c_d) # mass of the smallest highest-density region containing the true value ranks.append(np.asarray(jnp.mean(lq_draws > lq_true[:, None], axis=1))) ranks = np.concatenate(ranks) ax.plot(levels, [(ranks <= q).mean() for q in levels], lw=2, label=name) ax.set_xlabel("Nominal credibility level") ax.set_ylabel("Empirical coverage") ax.set_title("From scratch, 1 000 simulations") ax.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` NPE {'a': '154.66 ± 3.36', 'b': '6.14 ± 0.82', 's': '5.04 ± 3.45'} BNPE {'a': '154.54 ± 4.08', 'b': '6.08 ± 2.28', 's': '4.90 ± 4.08'} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](41. X @ coef)]))(jnp.linalg.lstsq(X, height)[0])", pydict(Dict("jnp" => jnp, "X" => X))) # Run Bayesian NPE ------------------------------------------------ m.npe(model, summary_stats = ols, num_simulations = 1_000, bayesian = true) # Summary and calibration ------------------------------------------------ m.summary() m.sbc_coverage(n_test = 200) ``` ::: ## Mathematical Details ### *Model* The model is the linear regression of [chapter 1](1.%20Linear%20Regression%20for%20continuous%20variable.qmd): $$ Y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\alpha + \beta X_i, \sigma) $$ $$ \alpha \sim \text{Normal}(178, 20), \qquad \beta \sim \text{LogNormal}(0, 1), \qquad \sigma \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 50) $$ NPE and BNPE only use it to simulate datasets $Y_i = \alpha + \beta X_i + \sigma \varepsilon_i$, $\varepsilon_i \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1)$, summarised by the least-squares estimates $s(Y) = (\hat\alpha, \hat\beta, \hat\sigma)$, which are sufficient for this model. The parameters are modelled in the unconstrained space $u = (\alpha,\ \log\beta,\ \text{logit}(\sigma/50))$, standardised with the training set, as described under *How NPE is trained*. ### *Neural posterior estimation* NPE fits the network parameters $\phi$ by minimizing the expected negative log-density of the parameters that generated each simulated dataset: $$ \hat\phi = \arg\min_\phi \; \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim p(\theta),\, x \sim p(x \mid \theta)}\left[-\log q_\phi\big(\theta \mid s(x)\big)\right] \approx \arg\min_\phi \; -\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M} \log q_\phi\big(\theta_j \mid s(x_j)\big) $$ This loss is the expected Kullback-Leibler divergence $\mathbb{E}_{p(x)}\big[\text{KL}\big(p(\theta \mid x)\,\|\,q_\phi(\theta \mid x)\big)\big]$ up to a constant, so it is minimized when $q_\phi(\theta \mid x) = p(\theta \mid x)$ for every $x$ [@papamakarios2016fast; @greenberg2019automatic]. This is why a single trained network is valid for all datasets (amortization). #### *Mixture density network* (`estimator="mdn"`) $$ q_\phi(u \mid s) = \sum_{c=1}^{C} \pi_c(s)\; \text{MVNormal}\big(u \mid \mu_c(s),\, L_c(s) L_c(s)^\top\big) $$ Where: - $C$ is the number of mixture components (`n_components`), and $D$ the number of (scalar) parameters. - A multilayer perceptron (`hidden` layers of BF's `m.bnn.layer_linear`, activation `activation`) maps $\tilde s$ to $h(\tilde s) \in \mathbb{R}^{C(1 + D + D(D+1)/2)}$ (`m.bnn.mixture_normal_size(C, D)` outputs). - The output layer `m.bnn.layer_mixture_normal` splits $h$ into $C$ logits, $C$ means $\mu_c \in \mathbb{R}^D$ and $C$ vectors of $D(D+1)/2$ values, and returns the BF mixture distribution with weights $\pi_c = \text{softmax}(\text{logits})_c$. - Each vector of $D(D+1)/2$ values becomes a lower-triangular Cholesky factor with `m.bnn.layer_cholesky`: the values fill the lower triangle row by row and the diagonal is made positive, $L_{c,dd} = \text{softplus}(h_{c,dd} + \delta) + 10^{-3}$, so every covariance matrix $L_c L_c^\top$ is valid. With $\delta = 0.5413$ (used by `m.npe()` and the from-scratch code), the diagonal starts at 1, the scale of the standardised parameters; the weights of the output layer are also initialised 10 times smaller than the other layers, so training starts close to a mixture of standard Normal distributions. #### *Normalizing flow* (`estimator="flow"`) The flow transforms $u$ into a standard Normal variable $z$ through `n_layers` affine coupling layers [@dinh2017density]. Each layer uses a binary mask $m$ (alternating between layers) and keeps the masked coordinates unchanged: $$ u' = m \odot u + (1 - m) \odot \big(u \odot e^{a(m \odot u,\, h)} + b(m \odot u,\, h)\big) $$ where $a(\cdot)$ and $b(\cdot)$ are outputs of a multilayer perceptron that sees only the unchanged coordinates and an embedding $h$ of the summary statistics, and $a = 2\tanh(\cdot/2)$ is bounded for stability. The Jacobian of each layer is triangular, so the density is $$ \log q_\phi(u \mid s) = \log \text{Normal}(z \mid 0, I) + \sum_{\text{layers}} \sum_{d} (1 - m_d)\, a_d $$ and sampling inverts the layers in reverse order, $u = \big(u' - b\big) \odot e^{-a}$ on the transformed coordinates. ### *Bayesian NPE* Bayesian NPE treats the network weights $\phi$ as unknown, with the simulations $\mathcal{D} = \{(u_j, s_j)\}$ as data [@delaunoy2024low]: $$ W^{(l)} \sim \text{Normal}\left(0, \frac{\sigma_\phi^2}{n_{in}^{(l)}}\right), \qquad b^{(l)} \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_\phi^2), \qquad p(\mathcal{D} \mid \phi) = \prod_{j=1}^{M} q_\phi(u_j \mid s_j) $$ where $n_{in}^{(l)}$ is the number of inputs of layer $l$ and $\sigma_\phi$ is `prior_scale`. The weight posterior is approximated by a mean-field Normal distribution $\hat p_\lambda(\phi) = \prod_k \text{Normal}(\phi_k \mid \mu_k, \sigma_k^2)$ that maximizes the evidence lower bound (stochastic variational inference, `svi_steps` Adam steps on mini-batches): $$ \text{ELBO}(\lambda) = \mathbb{E}_{\hat p_\lambda(\phi)}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{M} \log q_\phi(u_j \mid s_j) + \log p(\phi) - \log \hat p_\lambda(\phi)\right] $$ The means $\mu_k$ start at the weights of the trained standard network and the scales at $10^{-3}$. The posterior estimate averages the mixture densities of $S$ networks (`num_weight_samples`) drawn from $\hat p_\lambda$: $$ q(u \mid s) = \int q_\phi(u \mid s)\; p(\phi \mid \mathcal{D})\, d\phi \approx \frac{1}{S}\sum_{k=1}^{S} q_{\phi_k}(u \mid s), \qquad \phi_k \sim \hat p_\lambda(\phi) $$ and sampling draws an equal number of values from each network. When $\mathcal{D}$ is small, the weight posterior is wide and the mixture over networks widens the posterior estimate. The from-scratch code expresses both estimators with one BF model, $u_j \sim q_\phi(\cdot \mid s_j)$ with the weight priors above, and changes only the variational family of `m.svi`: - **NPE**: a point mass, $\hat p_\lambda(\phi) = \delta_{\hat\phi}$ (`AutoDelta`). The ELBO then reduces to $\sum_j \log q_{\hat\phi}(u_j \mid s_j) + \log p(\hat\phi)$, so SVI finds the posterior mode of the weights: the NPE loss plus a weight decay. - **Bayesian NPE**: a mean-field Normal (`AutoNormal`) whose means start at $\hat\phi$ and scales at $10^{-3}$. In both cases the likelihood of a mini-batch of 256 simulations is rescaled by $M/256$, and posterior draws for a dataset are predictions of the model, one $u$ per weight draw (`m.sample`). The densities needed for the expected coverage are $\log \frac{1}{S}\sum_k q_{\phi_k}(u \mid s)$, computed from the log-likelihood of the model under each weight draw. ### *Expected coverage* For $n$ test pairs $(\theta^*_i, x^*_i)$ simulated from the model (`n_test`), `m.sbc_coverage()` draws $K$ samples $u_{ik} \sim q(\cdot \mid s(x^*_i))$ (`n_post`) and computes the mass of the smallest highest-density region that contains the true value: $$ r_i = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathbb{1}\left[q(u_{ik} \mid s_i) > q(u^*_i \mid s_i)\right] $$ The true value lies inside the $(1-\alpha)$ highest-density region when $r_i \le 1 - \alpha$, so the empirical coverage at level $1-\alpha$ is $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \mathbb{1}[r_i \le 1 - \alpha]$ [@hermans2022trust]. A calibrated estimator has empirical coverage equal to $1-\alpha$ for every $\alpha$; a curve below the diagonal reveals over-confident posteriors, above the diagonal conservative ones. ## Notes ::: callout-note - NPE trades simulations for training: 20 000 simulations instead of the million used by ABC-SMC, but a network must be trained. It pays off when simulations are expensive or when many datasets must be analysed with the same model (amortization). - Two trainings of the same network (here `m.npe()` and the from-scratch code, which use the same settings but different random draws) give slightly different posteriors: over several seeds, both place the posterior means within about half an exact-posterior standard deviation of NUTS. This is the approximation error of a single trained network; more simulations reduce it. - An NPE posterior is only as good as the network fit. Always inspect the training curve (`m.sampler.plot_loss()`) and the expected coverage (`m.sbc_coverage()`) before interpreting the results. - The trained network is only valid for data similar to the simulations: observed data far outside the prior predictive distribution (model misspecification) give unreliable posteriors. - With 1 000 simulations, the standard NPE network is over-confident: its credible intervals contain the true parameters less often than their nominal level. Bayesian NPE is conservative: its intervals are too wide rather than too narrow, which is the safe side of the error, and both converge to the exact posterior as the simulation budget grows. - The BNPE posterior of the observed data is much wider than the exact one here: with 1 000 simulations, the network weights are poorly determined, and BNPE honestly reports this uncertainty. Increase `num_simulations` when simulations are affordable. - BNPE is slower than NPE, as it adds a variational fit of all network weights after the standard training. ::: ## Reference(s) @bishop1994mixture; @cranmer2020frontier; @delaunoy2024low; @dinh2017density; @greenberg2019automatic; @hermans2022trust; @papamakarios2016fast ::: {#refs} :::
